newsitem.title: USA: Air Force picks space missile finalists.
newsitem.headline: Air Force picks space missile finalists.

text.p: The Air Force selected McDonnell Douglas and Lockheed Martin divisions Friday as finalists for its $2 billion programme to replace all present Air Force space missiles with a new one to cut costs.
Air Force Secretary Sheila Widnall told a news conference that work already done showed "our goal of achieving a 25 percent to 50 percent savings in launch costs is realistic."
The new missile, now known only as the Evolved Expendable Launch Vehicle, is to replace the Air Force's present Atlas, Titan and Delta missiles as satellite launch vehicles in the next century.

Widnall announced that McDonnell Douglas Aerospace of Huntington Beach, Calif., and Lockheed Martin Corp.'s Astronautics Division near Denver had been awarded $60 million contracts to complete their competing models for the new missile.
She said one of them will be awarded contracts in mid-1998 to build the new missile, which will have medium- and heavy-lift versions.

The only real loser among the four contractors competing for the missile was Alliant Techsystems because the fourth was Boeing Defence and Space Group, and Boeing plans to merge with McDonnell Douglas.

Alliant President Richard Schwartz said that even though it lost in that competition it has won other work and remains on track to achieve its goal of increasing earnings per share at an average annual rate of 15 percent.

"The EELV programme was certainly a very significant opportunity and one that we wanted to win," Schwartz said in a statement. "However, it is only one of a number of large opportunities we have been pursuing."
The new rocket is part of President Clinton's space transportation plan, which calls for cheaper, faster space launches.
Other Air Force officials at the news conference said that although 50 percent savings in launch costs will be difficult to achieve, savings of 25 percent will not.

They said the savings will come from cutting the overhead costs for three different missile programmes to one, and from the cheaper costs of manufacturing only medium and heavy versions of one missile rather than three different missiles.
Medium and heavy versions of the missile will be able to put payloads from about 2,500 pounds to 45,000 pounds into a low Earth orbit, the Air Force said in a statement.

It said the medium-lift version was to be ready for its first launches from Vandenberg Air Force Base in California in 2001 and Cape Canaveral in Florida in 2002. The heavy lift version is to begin launches at Vandenberg in 2005 and Cape Canaveral in 2006, it said.
